record.paper_title: Statements and open problems on decidable sets X ⊆ N that contain informal notions and refer to the current knowledge on X
record.original_question: Are there infinitely many composite Fermat numbers, that is, infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^k) + 1 with k ∈ N?

evidence.quote: It is open whether or not there are infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^k) + 1, see [7, p. 159] and [11, p. 74].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For each non-negative integer $k$, the $k$-th Fermat number is defined by
$$F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1.$$
A Fermat number $F_k$ is called composite if it is not a prime. Determine whether there exist infinitely many non-negative integers $k$ such that $F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1$ is composite.
artifact.status_search_result: It is a classical and well-known open problem in number theory whether there are infinitely many composite Fermat numbers (equivalently, whether only finitely many Fermat primes exist). No proof in either direction is known; heuristic arguments suggest that only $F_0,\dots,F_4$ are prime, but this has not been established.

status_evidence.title: Fermat number - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is not known whether there are infinitely many Fermat primes or composite Fermat numbers.
status_evidence.claim: The question of whether infinitely many Fermat numbers are composite is open.
